meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Riches and honours acquired by unrighteousness are to me as a floating cloud'?
meta.ogDescription: A real one. Analects Book VII, verified in Legge's 1861 translation and the Chinese original 不義而富且貴，於我如浮雲.

answer.sourceLine: A genuine saying, recorded in the Analects, Book VII — chapter XV in James Legge’s numbering, and passage 16 in the Chinese Text Project’s ↗. The Chinese reads 不義而富且貴，於我如浮雲. One caveat worth carrying: these exact English words are Legge’s 1861 translation, not Confucius’s.

source.excerpt: The Master said, ‘With coarse rice to eat, with water to drink, and my bended arm for a pillow;—I have still joy in the midst of these things. Riches and honours acquired by unrighteousness, are to me as a floating cloud.’
trail: The line is chapter XV of Book VII in James Legge’s The Chinese Classics, Vol. I ↗, which prints the Chinese 不義而富且貴，於我如浮雲 with the English beside it.

The Chinese Text Project ↗ carries the same passage as number 16 of 述而 (Shù ér), pairing the identical Chinese with Legge’s English. The chapter numbering of Book VII differs between editions; the text does not.
Project Gutenberg’s free text of Legge’s Analects ↗ prints it at Book VII, Chapter XV in exactly these words — a third independent copy of the same translation.
Quote Investigator’s Confucius file ↗ has never needed to investigate this one. Its Confucius entries are all sayings pinned on him by mistake, and this is not among them.
source.excerptNote: Legge prints a comma after “unrighteousness”; the form that circulates online drops it. (Watch the spelling too — Legge sets “honours”, while the Chinese Text Project’s copy of his English Americanises it to “honors”.)

source.rightsNote: Both layers are free to use. The Chinese original is an ancient text, and this English wording comes from James Legge’s The Chinese Classics, Vol. I — first published 1861 and revised in 1893, so comfortably before the 1931 US public-domain cutoff ↗. Note that copyright rides on the translation, not the sage: a modern English rendering of the same passage is a separate work with its own rights, so quote Legge’s version if you want it free and clear.

author.name: Confucius
author.heading: Who Confucius actually was
author.metaLine: 551–479 BC · Chinese philosopher & teacher, state of Lu
author.bio: Confucius was a philosopher and teacher of the Spring and Autumn period, from the state of Lu in what is now Qufu, Shandong. He did not write the Analects himself — his sayings were gathered by disciples and later followers many years after his death, which is why almost every “Confucius quote” is really a quotation from that compilation, and, in English, from a translator on top of it. His teaching centred on virtue, ritual propriety and the cultivation of character over material advantage, which is exactly the ground this line stands on.

misattribution.heading: Real quote, dangerous neighbourhood
misattribution.intro: This one is authentic — which, for Confucius, makes it the exception. His name is one of the internet’s most abused attributions, so the useful warnings here are about the company this line keeps, and about whose English you are actually quoting.

items.why: “Riches and honours acquired by unrighteousness” is English chosen by a Scottish missionary-scholar for an 1861 edition. What Confucius said was 不義而富且貴，於我如浮雲 — eleven characters, as the Chinese Text Project prints them ↗. Credit the sentiment to Confucius; credit the phrasing to Legge.

items.who: “Choose a job you love, and you will never have to work a day in your life”
items.why: Stamped with Confucius’s name everywhere and absent from the Analects. Quote Investigator ↗ concludes that “the linkage to Confucius appears to be spurious,” tracing the saying to a 1982 Princeton Alumni Weekly piece and finding the first Confucius credit in Computerworld in June 1985.

items.who: “The journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step”
items.why: Wikiquote files this among the misattributions ↗, crediting it to Laozi in the Tao Te Ching — and does the same for “I hear and I forget. I see and I remember. I do and I understand,” which it assigns to Xunzi.
Sold as Confucian wisdom, but he argued against it. The World of Chinese ↗ notes his actual position was 以直报怨，以德报德 — repay injustice with justice, and repay good with good.

misattribution.truthLine: The test that settles all of it is simply to open the book. This line is right there in Book VII ↗. Most of the famous ones are not.

context.heading: Why a cloud?
lead: The sentence lands harder when you read the whole paragraph. Confucius has just described a life of coarse rice, plain water and a bent arm for a pillow, and said he finds joy in the middle of it. Only then does he wave off wealth won by cheating — and notice that he does not wave it off as a temptation heroically resisted.

That is the force of 浮雲, a floating cloud: not evil, just weightless. Riches taken dishonestly do not scandalise him, they simply drift past overhead, belonging to somebody else’s sky. It is a much cooler, stranger line than the moralising it usually gets flattened into.
context.detailsSummary: The numbering, and whose English you are reading
detailsBody: Book VII of the Analects is 述而 (Shù ér), named the way all twenty books are — after its own opening words, 述而不作, ‘a transmitter and not a maker.’ The Chinese Text Project ↗ lists it by that romanisation alone, as ‘Shu Er’, and so does Legge. Its chapter numbering is not stable across editions: Legge prints this passage as chapter XV, while the Chinese Text Project lists the identical text as number 16. That is why you will see the same sentence cited as both Analects 7.15 and 7.16 — neither is wrong.

James Legge (1815–1897) produced The Chinese Classics across the 1860s and 70s, with Volume I ↗ — the Analects, the Great Learning and the Doctrine of the Mean — appearing in 1861 and again in a revised edition in 1893. His register is the reason so many Confucius quotations sound faintly biblical in English. Eleven characters of terse classical Chinese become “riches and honours acquired by unrighteousness”: accurate, but unmistakably Victorian.
